validated_results.title: Alcohol drinking and renal cell carcinoma in women and men.
validated_results.journal: European journal of cancer prevention : the official journal of the European Cancer Prevention Organisation (ECP)
validated_results.reason: Hospital-based case-control study reporting sex-specific odds ratios for alcohol drinking and incident histologically confirmed renal cell carcinoma.

extraction.population: Incident renal cell cancer cases and hospital controls in northern Italy

sample_size.excerpt: The role of alcohol consumption on the risk of renal cell cancer was investigated separately for women and men, in a case-control study of 348 people with incident histologically confirmed cancer and 1048 hospital controls from northern Italy.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 348 + 1048 = 1396

cases.excerpt: The role of alcohol consumption on the risk of renal cell cancer was investigated separately for women and men, in a case-control study of 348 people with incident histologically confirmed cancer and 1048 hospital controls from northern Italy.

effect_size.excerpt: The odds ratios were 1.2 (95% confidence interval, 0.6-2.4) for the highest tertile of intake in women (>or=3 drinks per day) and 0.8 (0.4-1.3) for the highest quartile of intake in men (>or=6 drinks per day).

validated_results.journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort reporting a relative risk for highest versus lowest quartile of total soyfood intake and incident bladder cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest quartile of energy-adjusted total soy intake (>=92.5 g/1000 Kcal) vs lowest quartile (<36.9 g/1000 Kcal)

sample_size.excerpt: As of December 31, 2000, 329,848 person-years of follow-up were accrued.

cases.excerpt: Sixty-one histologically confirmed incident bladder cancer cases were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: Relative to the lowest quartile of energy-adjusted total soy intake (<36.9 g/1000 Kcal), the highest quartile of total soy intake (> or =92.5 g/1000 Kcal) was associated with a 2.3-fold increase in bladder cancer risk (95% confidence interval = 1.1-5.1) after adjustment for cigarette smoking and level of education.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Relative to the lowest quartile of energy-adjusted total soy intake (<36.9 g/1000 Kcal), the highest quartile of total soy intake (> or =92.5 g/1000 Kcal) was associated with a 2.3-fold increase in bladder cancer risk (95% confidence interval = 1.1-5.1) after adjustment for cigarette smoking and level of education.
